name: Mannarasala Sree Nagaraja Temple
tagline: Kerala’s largest living serpent grove, famous for its naga idols and women‑centred priestly tradition
summary: Mannarasala Sree Nagaraja Temple (Haripad, Alappuzha) is a living kavu shrine for serpent worship, known for thousands of naga idols, the Mannarasala Amma and fertility rites.
description: Mannarasala is a working serpent‑god shrine set inside a living kavu (sacred grove) beside the ancestral Mannarasala Illam near Haripad in Alappuzha district. The grove contains very many stone, metal and clay serpent images placed along shaded paths and under trees.

Devotional life at Mannarasala blends Vedic and local naga rituals (Noorum Palum, Uruli Kamazhthal, Sarpabali and Sarpam Pattu) and centres on the hereditary Mannarasala Illam. The temple issues darshan windows and runs an online vazhipad (offering) portal; visitors should treat the site as an active place of worship and follow the temple’s rules.

history.significance: Mannarasala is a principal centre of naga worship in Kerala and a rare major shrine whose chief ritual role is vested in the eldest woman of the Mannarasala Illam (the Mannarasala Amma).

timeline.event: Parasurama consecrates Sree Nagaraja at the site and establishes serpent worship at Mannarasala (traditional account).
The temple records continuous observance of Sarpam‑related rites since 1073 M.E. (Malayalam Era) as part of its liturgical chronology.
Records show a Sarpam Pattu observance in 1151 M.E. (listed on the temple festivals page; converted here to 1976 C.E.).
Umadevi Antharjanam was anointed Mannarasala Amma (chief priestess) — a well‑reported modern anointment; she later died in August 2023.

keyFacts: The living grove and temple compound are commonly described in published sources as covering roughly 16 acres.
The temple publishes daily darshan times and an online booking portal for authorised offerings; the official site lists 51 offerings and sample rates — confirm timings and charges before travelling.

folklore.title: Parasurama, the grateful Nagaraja and the Mannarasala Illam
story: By temple tradition, the land that became Kerala was reclaimed by Parasurama but remained barren and was infested with snakes. On Shiva’s advice Parasurama propitiates the chief serpent‑king (Nagaraja). Nagaraja makes the soil fertile and remains at Mannarasala to protect the land.

A household tradition of the Mannarasala Illam tells of a childless Brahmin couple, Vasudeva and Sreedevi, who rescue wounded snakes after a forest fire. In gratitude Nagaraja promises to be reborn in their house. Tradition says a five‑hooded serpent first appeared as a child and then took up residence in the Illam’s Nilavara (sacred cellar); this promise underpins the Illam’s hereditary, women‑centred priesthood and the annual rituals.
folklore.note: Versions and emphasis vary between the temple’s published account, regional press stories and scholarly descriptions; the above follows the temple’s history while noting that other accounts abridge or frame details differently.

spiritual.summary: Mannarasala’s sacred atmosphere arises from the grove, the many serpent images and family‑led rituals. Devotion mixes Vedic rites and local naga practices; many devotees petition for fertility, healing or to fulfil vows.

experiences.title: Amma darshan and simple offerings
experiences.text: Attend an Amma darshan window or a common offering (Noorum Palum / Palpayasam). The temple posts Amma darshan times and many offerings are bookable online or at the vazhipad counter; confirm and book in advance for a specific seva.

experiences.title: Quiet walk through the kavu
experiences.text: Walk the designated paths through the sacred grove to view stone and metal serpent images, sit in silence near the trees and observe local devotees. Stay on marked routes and do not touch idols or ritual items.

experiences.title: Witness festival rites (Ayilyam and processions)
experiences.text: When Ayilyam-related days and the Ezhunnallathu (procession) occur, idols are carried to the Illam and special rites such as Noorum Palum and Uruli Kamazhthal are performed — these are crowded, highly ritualised events with restricted access in parts.

spiritual.bestFor: Devotees seeking naga propitiation or fertility rites; people studying Kerala’s sacred‑grove culture and vernacular ritual arts; respectful visitors who accept active worship.
mindfulTips: Confirm Amma darshan windows and vazhipad availability on the temple’s official site before you travel.
Dress modestly in line with Hindu temple customs; follow instructions from temple staff and the darshan counters.
Photography and videography inside the compound are prohibited except by prior written permission — obey posted signs and staff directions.
Do not enter protected kavu areas; keep to designated paths and avoid touching idols, ritual vessels or offerings.

highlights: The sacred grove (kavu) and shaded paths lined with many serpent images — the essential visual and devotional experience.
The Mannarasala Illam and the Nilavara (sacred cellar) beside the temple, linked to the Illam’s ancestral custodianship of the shrine.
Ayilyam festival observances (Thulam Ayilyam and other Aayilyam days) when idols are carried in procession to the Illam and special rites are performed.
Distinctive women‑centred priesthood: the Mannarasala Amma, a hereditary female head of the Illam, performs central ritual duties.

visitorInfo.bestTime: The cooler, drier months (roughly October–February) are easiest for travel. Ayilyam festival days (in Kanni, Thulam and Kumbham months) are most dramatic but very crowded; confirm festival dates and darshan arrangements before travelling.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Mannarasala is beside Haripad town in Alappuzha district. The nearest railway station is Haripad (HAD), a short road distance from the temple. Haripad has frequent KSRTC and private bus connections; Cochin (COK) and Trivandrum (TRV) airports are the nearest international airports with road transfers of a few hours.
etiquette: Dress modestly in accordance with temple custom; follow staff instructions about specific dress (many visitors wear saree/salwar for women and mundu/dhoti for men where asked).
Photography and videography are strictly prohibited inside the compound except with prior written permission from the temple.
Buy authorised offerings only from the temple’s vazhipad counters or the official online portal; follow counter instructions for puja procedures.
Do not enter protected kavu areas, do not touch idols, ritual vessels or offerings, and observe silence in worship areas.
visitorInfo.duration: Allow about 1–2 hours for a focused visit; plan longer for a booked seva or during festivals.

byTrain: Haripad (station code HAD) — nearest station (approx. 2–4 km from Mannarasala). Check Indian Railways/station enquiry for current timetables.
byBus: Haripad KSRTC stand and private bus services — frequent connections to Alappuzha, Kayamkulam and nearby towns; the bus/stand is a short drive from the temple.
byWater: No regular ferry serves Mannarasala directly. Nearest major backwater terminals are at Alappuzha (Alleppy); combine with a road transfer from the backwater hubs as required.
byAir: Cochin International Airport (COK) — approx. 114–120 km by road (allow roughly 2–3 hours depending on route and traffic).
Trivandrum International Airport (TRV) — approx. 140 km by road (allow roughly 2–3 hours).
